segments.title: Why commanders stood in exposed positions
segments.summary: Mikasa's exposed command position shows why admirals and commanding officers accepted personal danger to gain the best possible view before radar and electronic sensors.
segments.body: Mikasa's command position appears dangerously exposed for a place occupied by admirals and senior officers during battle. Its advantage was the wide field of view. Before radar and electronic sensors, commanders depended heavily on what lookouts and their own senses could tell them. They could remain in a protected room below and receive reports, but standing above gave them direct access to the changing scene. The choice also carried a moral interpretation: an officer seeking the best information should accept greater personal risk. Sandbags offered some protection without removing the danger. The post is then linked to a battle whose effects are described as lasting into the following century.

evidence.note: He explains that the exposed position maximized visual information before radar and contrasts it with a protected command room.

segments.title: Mikasa's command post as a place of decision
segments.summary: Mikasa's preserved command post prompts a personal reflection on the weight of decisions made there, qualified by the possibility that the feeling comes from prior reading and imagination.
segments.body: After the tactical explanation, the command post prompts a more personal response. The preserved position feels like a place where choices carried unusual weight. That impression is explicitly qualified: it may come from prior reading and imagination rather than from anything the site can prove by itself. Even with that caveat, the moment shows how a preserved warship can connect written history with the physical conditions in which officers observed events and made decisions. The recommendation to visit Mikasa follows directly from that experience.

evidence.note: He says the post feels like a point of decision, while acknowledging that the feeling may partly be his own interpretation.
